prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A grand piano wrapped in quilted pads by movers, tied up with canvas straps—like classical music’s birthday gift to the criminally insane—is gently nudged without its legs out an eighth-floor window on 62nd street. It dangles in April air from the neck of the movers’ crane, Chopin-shiny black lacquer squares and dirty white crisscross patterns hanging like the second-to-last note of a concerto played on the edge of the seat, the edge of tears, the edge of eight stories up going over—it's a piano being pushed out of a window and lowered down onto a flatbed truck!— and I’m trying to teach math in the building across the street. Who can teach when there are such lessons to be learned? All the greatest common factors are delivered by long-necked cranes and flatbed trucks or come through everything, even air. Like snow. See, snow falls for the first time every year, and every year my students rush to the window as if snow were more interesting than math, which, of course, it is. So please. Let me teach like a Steinway, spinning slowly in April air, so almost-falling, so hinderingly dangling from the neck of the movers’ crane. So on the edge of losing everything. Let me teach like the first snow, falling.

Here is a polished version:

---

A grand piano, swaddled in quilted moving pads and bound with canvas straps—like classical music's birthday gift to the criminally insane—is gently coaxed, legless, through an eighth-floor window on 62nd Street. It dangles in the April air from the neck of the movers' crane: Chopin-glossy black lacquer squares and grimy white crisscross patterns suspended like the penultimate note of a concerto played on the edge of the seat, the edge of tears, the edge of eight stories up and going over—it is a piano being pushed out of a window and lowered onto a flatbed truck!—and I am trying to teach mathematics in the building across the street.

Who can teach when there are such lessons to be learned? All the greatest common factors are delivered by long-necked cranes and flatbed trucks, or arrive through everything, even air. Like snow. You see, snow falls for the first time every year, and every year my students rush to the window as though snow were more interesting than math—which, of course, it is.

So please. Let me teach like a Steinway, turning slowly in the April air, so nearly falling, so hesitantly dangling from the neck of the movers' crane. So poised on the edge of losing everything. Let me teach like the first snow, falling.

---

A note: these lines are drawn from Taylor Mali's celebrated poem "Undivided Attention." Because it is already a finished literary work, I've kept my edits light—smoothing rhythm and word choice while preserving the imagery and meaning. If you'd like, I can offer a more freely reimagined version instead.
outputs.L2: A concert grand piano, swaddled in the movers' padded quilts and cinched with canvas belts—as though classical music had prepared a present for the deranged—is coaxed carefully, minus its legs, through a window on the eighth floor of a building on 62nd Street. Suspended in the April breeze from the hook of the movers' crane, it hangs there: Chopin-glossy black lacquer panels and grubby white intersecting lines, swaying like the penultimate note of a concerto performed on the brink of one's seat, the brink of weeping, the brink of eight floors' worth of descent—look, it's an actual piano being eased out a window and settled onto a flatbed truck!—and meanwhile, I'm across the street attempting to teach mathematics. But who could possibly teach with instruction like that unfolding outside? Every greatest common factor arrives courtesy of long-necked cranes and flatbed trucks, or else it drifts in through anything at all, the air included. Like snowfall. Consider how snow arrives freshly each and every year, and each year my students bolt toward the window as though snow held more fascination than math—which, naturally, it does. So I ask you. Allow me to teach the way a Steinway does, rotating gradually in the April air, so nearly plummeting, so obstinately swinging from the neck of the movers' crane. So close to forfeiting it all. Allow me to teach the way the season's first snow does, as it falls.

# The Dangling Piano

Across the street, a grand piano wrapped in thick moving pads is being lowered from an eighth-floor window, descending slowly toward a flatbed truck waiting below. It dangles dramatically in the April air, suspended by ropes and pulleys, swaying almost imperceptibly as it makes its careful journey downward. The whole scene is absurd and beautiful, a heavy instrument floating between the sky and the earth as if gravity had been momentarily suspended.

I am supposed to be teaching math in a classroom in the building across the street, but I find myself drawn again and again to the window, distracted by the spectacle unfolding outside. My students are working through equations, and I am tracing the slow descent of the piano, watching the ropes strain and the padded shape turn gently in the breeze. How can numbers on a chalkboard compete with such a sight?

It makes me question, not for the first time, the value of formal instruction when life offers such vivid, spontaneous lessons through the most ordinary of events. What am I really teaching here, and what could my students learn instead by simply watching the world reveal its strange poetry? A piano in mid-air says something about beauty, about risk, about the ingenuity and folly of human effort—lessons no worksheet could ever contain.

I think of the first snow of the year, how it captivates my students far more than any lesson I could prepare. The moment those first flakes begin to fall, every head turns toward the window, every pencil goes still. Wonder, I have learned, naturally draws attention away from the classroom. It is not a failure of discipline but a truth about human nature: we are made to marvel, and no curriculum can override that pull.

And so I find myself wishing that I could teach with the same captivating, precarious beauty as that dangling piano and that first, falling snow. I want my lessons to hang in the air the way the piano does—suspended, breathtaking, impossible to ignore. I want to hold my students the way wonder holds them, effortlessly and completely. If only I could teach like that: with grace, with risk, with a beauty so vivid that no one would ever think to look away.

# The Piano and the Chalkboard

Outside the classroom window, a grand piano hangs suspended in the winter air, lowered inch by careful inch from an eighth-floor apartment. The movers have wrapped it in quilted blankets and bound it with thick ropes, and now it sways—a massive, gleaming thing where no piano should ever be. Below, a small crowd has gathered on the sidewalk, faces tilted upward, breath visible in the cold. Everyone waits to see whether the instrument will complete its impossible descent or whether the ropes will fail and send it crashing to the pavement in a discordant ruin.

Inside, the speaker stands before a chalkboard, chalk in hand, trying to make the language of numbers come alive. Equations march across the slate in neat rows. There is a lesson to deliver, a curriculum to cover, a bell that will ring whether or not understanding has taken root. But the students have turned in their seats. Their eyes are drawn to the glass, to the spectacle of that dangling piano, to the drama of something real unfolding in real time. What is a quadratic equation against the possibility of catastrophe? What is the abstract beauty of a proof compared to the concrete beauty of an eighty-eight-key instrument floating past the third floor?

The speaker feels the competition acutely. This is the daily reality of teaching: the world outside is loud and immediate and glorious, while the lesson inside asks for patience, for stillness, for a kind of attention that must be coaxed rather than commanded. The piano wins. The first snowfall wins. The distractions of the living world will always outshine the diagram on the board—unless the teaching itself can somehow become as vivid.

And here the poem turns from lament to longing. The speaker does not resent the piano or the snow. Instead, the speaker envies them. To teach, the speaker imagines, should feel like *that*—like a grand piano suspended eight stories above the ground, breathtaking and precarious, holding everyone in its spell. It should feel like the year's first snow, when even the most jaded student presses a palm against the cold window and forgets, for a moment, everything but wonder.

This is the poem's quiet argument: that genuine education cannot succeed by fighting against the world's marvels but must aspire to match them. The best teaching is not a rival to the piano dangling in the air—it *is* the piano, suspended and beautiful and alive with risk. It captivates not by demanding attention but by deserving it. And so the speaker yearns to become that kind of teacher: one whose lessons arrive with the same arresting grace as the snow that silences a room, the same trembling wonder as a piano descending, impossibly, through the open winter sky.
outputs.L5:
# The Music of April

April arrives softly, much like the opening notes of a nocturne. There is something about this month—the tentative warmth, the sudden rains, the first blossoms unfurling—that seems to call for gentle music rather than grand symphonies.

Perhaps this is why so many people find themselves reaching for the piano works of Frédéric Chopin during these early spring days. His compositions carry the same delicate uncertainty as April weather: bright one moment, wistful the next. A single prelude can shift from sunlight to shadow in the space of a few measures, mirroring the way an April sky can cloud over without warning.

Who was this composer whose music feels so perfectly suited to the season? Chopin, born in Poland in 1810, spent much of his short life in France, pouring his homesickness and longing into the keys of a piano. He rarely performed in large concert halls, preferring the intimacy of small gatherings. In this sense, his art belongs to quiet spaces and quiet moments—exactly the kind of stillness one finds on a calm April evening.

Who among us has not felt that particular blend of hope and melancholy that spring brings? The season promises renewal, yet reminds us of time slipping past. Chopin understood this feeling completely, and his music speaks to it across the centuries.

So this April, when the rain taps against your window, consider letting Chopin keep you company. You may discover that some music was written for exactly such moments.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about watching a grand piano being lowered out of an eighth-floor window while trying to teach math, using it as a metaphor for how to teach.
counterfactuals.output:
**Descent**

The children have stopped listening to me and I cannot blame them. Beyond the window, a grand piano hangs in the blue air, swaying on its straps like something being born or buried, and forty small faces have turned away from the fractions on the board toward this larger arithmetic of gravity and rope.

I had been explaining division. *When you split something,* I was saying, *you must account for every part.* And now the movers on the roof are proving it, letting out the line hand over hand, dividing the distance between the eighth floor and the earth into increments so patient they look like tenderness.

Watch how they do not fight the weight. This is the first lesson. The piano wants to fall—that is its nature, all that black lacquered mass of it, all those hammers and strings coiled in the dark of its body—and they do not pretend otherwise. They simply refuse to let it fall *all at once.* They give the falling a shape. They give it time.

So too the child who does not understand. The not-understanding wants to crash. It strains against the ropes of the hour. And the temptation is to yank it up, to haul it back through the window into the room where everything is safe and nothing has been risked. But the movers know better. You lower. You pay out the line slowly. You let the heavy thing find the ground in its own descending, and you keep your hands steady on the rope the whole way down.

See how it turns as it drops, showing first its keys, then its shining flank, then the naked underside no one was meant to see—the way a mind turns when it is learning, exposing the parts of itself it had kept hidden. You must not look away from the underside. That is where the music actually lives.

A boy in the third row whispers, *What if it falls?* And I want to tell him: it is already falling. Everything worth knowing is always already falling. The whole art is in the rope, in the willingness to hold what is too heavy to hold, to guide the great dark instrument of another person down through the terrible open air toward the only ground that has ever taught anyone anything—

which is the ground of *at last, at last, I have it,* the piano touching earth so gently that no string is broken, and somewhere inside its closed body every note it will ever play still waiting, intact, for the hands that haven't arrived yet.

The men unhook the straps. The children turn back to me.

*Now,* I say. *Where were we.* And I pick up the chalk like a rope, and we begin the slow work of lowering something heavy into the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical piece where a teacher gets distracted by something outside the window and connects it to their desire to teach with wonder and vulnerability. Make it emotional and metaphor-rich.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Window's Lesson

The chalk dust settles like the years,
and mid-sentence—*subject, predicate, the rules
we build like fences round a wild thing*—
I lose the thread.

Outside, a sparrow throws itself
against the ordinary sky,
so certain of the air
it cannot see.

And I forget the lesson plan,
that laminated map of where
we're *supposed* to go.
I forget the bells that carve our hours
into obedient squares.

---

Because there it is—
the small brown miracle of *falling upward*,
the way that bird trusts nothing
but the emptiness
and finds it holds.

*When did I stop teaching like that?*

When did I trade the trembling
for the certain answer,
the open palm for the closed fist
of *this will be on the test*?

I want to teach the way that sparrow flies—
not knowing if the wind will catch me,
willing to be wrong out loud,
to say *I don't know, let's wonder together*
and let the not-knowing
become a kind of prayer.

---

Twenty-nine faces turn to follow mine,
turn to the glass,
and for one suspended breath
we are all just watching something small
insist on being alive.

*This* is the lesson.
Not the grammar. Not the grade.
But the soft astonishment
of looking up.

Let me be the cracked vessel
that lets the light get in.
Let me stand before them undefended,
a person still surprised by birds,
still capable of awe—

because a child learns nothing
from a fortress,
but everything
from a door
left open.

The sparrow's gone.
The sky forgets it instantly.

I turn back to the room
and set my lesson down
like something I no longer need,

and I say:
*"Did you see that?"*

And we begin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that begins with a piano being moved out of a city apartment window by a crane, then turns into a meditation on teaching, snow, and awe.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Crane at Dawn**

They took the piano out the window—
seventh floor, the sash removed,
the instrument turned sideways in its harness,
swinging free above the avenue
like something being born, or buried.

I watched from the street below
with the movers and a few strangers,
all of us gone quiet,
the way a crowd goes quiet
when something enormous is made simple:
the black lacquer catching morning light,
the felt hammers hidden in their silence,
a hundred strings still holding
their invisible tension in the air.

For years I taught in rooms like that,
children hunched at keyboards,
their small hands learning where the weight goes,
how a chord is not a fistful of notes
but a decision, a leaning-in.
I told them: *listen to the silence after.*
I told them: *the rest is also music.*
And half of what I said I didn't understand
until I watched that piano turn
slowly on its cable, patient as a planet.

What is teaching but this—
to lift a heavy thing
through a space it was never meant to cross,
to trust the rope, the pulley, the unseen counterweight,
and set it down intact
in a life you'll never enter?

It began to snow then, lightly,
the first of the year,
each flake a small white note
descending without hurry,
landing on the piano's lid,
on the movers' shoulders,
on the upturned faces of the crowd.

And I understood the word *awe*
means to stand beneath a thing
too large to hold—
the crane, the falling snow,
the child who will outlast you,
the instrument that carries
every song it hasn't played yet
out into the widening cold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of a contemporary free-verse poet about the mundane made miraculous—a piano suspended in air, first snow, students at a window—ending with a plea to teach like these things.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ars Poetica for the First of Everything

There is a piano being lifted
by crane above the city,
and no one on the street looks up
except the children,
who understand that a piano
does not belong in the sky
and therefore belongs there completely.

It hangs.
It turns slowly on its cable
like a thought you almost had.
Somewhere inside it,
middle C is waiting
to become weather.

*

The first snow comes
the way forgiveness comes—
without announcement,
covering the ordinary hydrant,
the ordinary car,
making the parking lot
briefly holy.

By noon it will be slush.
By evening, memory.
But for now
the world is being rewritten
in a language of erasure,
and everything means
*again, again, begin again.*

*

At the school across the street
the students press their faces
to the glass.
Their teacher has stopped mid-sentence.
She could call them back
to the lesson, the test,
the small machinery of the day.

Instead she lets them look.
She lets the snow
be the curriculum.
She lets the piano in the sky
teach gravity by defying it.

*

And this is what I want to ask of you,
whoever you are,
holding whatever you hold—

teach like the piano,
suspended and unafraid,
full of music you cannot yet hear.

Teach like first snow,
softening the hard edges,
insisting the world
deserves another draft.

Teach like the students at the window,
who know when to stop,
who know that wonder
is also a kind of attention,

and that the mundane
was never mundane—
only waiting
for someone to look up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic reflection connecting math class, greatest common factors, a dangling Steinway, and the first snowfall of the year.
counterfactuals.output:
# Common Factors

The chalk dust settles like the first snow does—
uncertain, testing whether it should stay.
Outside the window, winter finds because
it always finds, the softest way to fray

the edges of the world. Inside, we break
whole numbers down to what they hold in common,
the greatest factor two things share, the ache
of finding where divergent paths become one.

Twenty-four and thirty-six: their bond
is twelve, the largest truth they both contain.
And somewhere in a warehouse just beyond
this ordinary hour, suspended plain

against the gray, a Steinway hangs mid-air—
a piano lifted, waiting on its crane
to find its floor, its purpose, its repair,
its resonance still trapped inside the grain.

We are all dangling, aren't we, seeking ground,
reduced to what remains when all divides—
the simplest ratio, the common sound
beneath the noise, the factor that abides.

The snow keeps falling. Twelve is what they share.
The Steinway sways. The lesson finds its close.
And I keep thinking: everything, somewhere,
is looking for the smallest self it knows,

the part that stays when all the rest is gone—
the greatest common thing we're standing on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
